fetched_contents.text: Effect of oral antiseptics in reducing SARS-CoV-2 infectivity: evidence from a randomized double-blind clinical trial ABSTRACT Background: In vitro studies have shown that several oral antiseptics have virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2. Thus, mouthwashes have been proposed as an easy to implement strategy to reduce viral transmission. However, there are no data measuring SARS-CoV-2 viability after mouthwashes in vivo. Methods: In this randomized double-blind, five-parallel-group, placebo-controlled clinical trial, SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load (by quantitative PCR) and its infectious capacity (incubating saliva in cell cultures) have been evaluated before and after four different antiseptic mouthwashes and placebo in 54 COVID-19 patients. Results: Contrary to in vitro evidence, salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes. Viral culture indicated that cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) significantly reduced viral infectivity, but only at 1-hour post-mouthwash. Conclusion: These results indicate that some of the mouthwashes currently used to reduce viral infectivity are not efficient in vivo and, furthermore, that this effect is not immediate, generating a false sense of security. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT04707742.. KEYWORDS: SARS-CoV-2, saliva, COVID-19, infectivity, mouthwash Introduction The Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has already infected more than 530 million people and has caused almost 6,3 million deaths globally [1] in 2 years. In addition to vaccination, therapeutic strategies must also be pursued, as they are essential to stop the severity of the disease and the spread of the virus. Transmission of the virus occurs by respiratory route (aerosols and respiratory droplets) and by contact with contaminated surfaces followed by contact with nasal, oral or ocular mucosa [2]. Transmission can happen in pre-symptomatic, symptomatic or asymptomatic patients [3]. Therefore, prevention practices such as the use of masks, hands’ hygiene and social distancing remain the key pillars of public infection control to avoid contagion. The detection rate of virus in the saliva of COVID-19 patients reaches 91.7% [4] thus recognizing saliva as a valid substrate for the detection of SARS-CoV-2 [5]. This also implies that direct or indirect contact with saliva represents a risk of COVID-19 transmission. This is very relevant for the general population but especially risky for professionals with direct access to the oral cavity such as dentists, ENT (Ear Nose and Throat) and cervicofacial surgery specialists, or maxillofacial surgeons. For these reasons, various health authorities have suggested the use of antiseptic mouthwashes by patients as an infection control measure prior to the procedure [6]. However, the above recommendations are not supported on evidence-based clinical data. There is a considerable number of publications in the literature studying the in vitro effect on viral load of different oral antiseptics which are part of mouth rinses [7–14]. However, there is still a disparity of results between studies, even contradicting each other's postulates. In addition, there are few clinical studies available, with strong design flaws such as lack of a control group or pilot studies with extremely low samples sizes [15–18]. In addition, all these clinical studies assess viral load reduction based on RT-qPCR results, without taking into account the effect of the mouthwash on viral infectivity. For example, in a recent clinical study, none of the four mouthwashes tested reduced total viral load as measured by RT-qPCR in saliva, but it is unknown if any of the residual viral genome equivalents detected are infectious [19]. Culturing SARS-CoV-2 from saliva samples has proven to be technically challenging [17], and therefore it has been difficult to evaluate viral infectivity in vivo after the use of oral antiseptics. It is therefore necessary to build on established knowledge to demonstrate the actual effectiveness of different mouthwashes on viral load, including their effect on viral infectivity. In the current manuscript, the results from a randomized, double-blind, five-parallel-group, placebo-controlled clinical trial where the effect of four different oral antiseptics is evaluated both by RT-qPCR (total viral load) and for the first time by infection of the saliva samples in cell cultures (infectious viral load). Mouthwash products and concentrations were selected based on previous efficacy studies in in vitro studies [7–14] and products’ commercial availability, in order to facilitate direct use during the pandemic. Thus, the purpose of our study was not to compare equivalent concentrations of antiseptics, but to test efficacy for already-developed formulations. The results were compared to a placebo group where participants performed the same mouthwash with water, establishing a comprehensive evaluation of the efficacy of the different compounds tested, and therefore their potential to reduce SARS-CoV-2 transmission. fetched_contents.text: Reduction of SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load with pre-procedural mouth rinses: a randomised, controlled, clinical trial Introduction Considering the role of the oral cavity in the pathogenicity and transmission of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2)1,2 and the routine aerosol-generating nature of procedures in dentistry,3 dental providers and oral surgeons are at particular high risk of COVID-19 transmission.1,4,5,6 During the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, dentists and other healthcare professionals who work in the oral cavity have implemented the use of mouth rinses to reduce viral loads as recommended by the American Dental Association (ADA). Prophylactic rinses are commonly used before routine procedures like dental fillings and cleanings, or before surgeries requiring intubation.7 By disinfecting the oral cavity through bacteriostatic, bactericidal and virucidal rinses, practitioners seek to mitigate the risk of spreading an infection from a patient's mouth to other parts of their body or to the outside environment. Therapeutic mouthwashes which contain active ingredients, such as chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), povidone-iodine (PI), or alcohol-based Listerine, are commonly used in dentistry. Existing data provide evidence for their efficacy in reducing bacterial and viral loads in in vitro cell cultures,8,9,10,11 oral cavities12 and aerosols13,14 generated during procedures. Recent systematic reviews also strongly support the hypothesis that prophylactic rinses can be effective in reducing the oral viral load of SARS-Cov-2.2,4,15 At the time of this study design, there was little empirical data to support pre-procedural rinses to reduce COVID-19 transmission to healthcare professionals or patients.12,16,17 Currently, the ADA states that evidence supports pre-procedural mouth rinses as effective in reducing oral viral load, but this has not been directly proven to reduce in-office spread of viruses and more research is needed.18 It is imperative to know if a reduction in viral loads lasts for a clinically meaningful duration that would provide a safe window to conduct routine procedures.19 While in vitro experiments provide controlled information, we attempted to best mimic the in vivo environments encountered in a healthcare setting during oral procedures. Hence, we conducted a prospective, parallel groups, randomised, double-blind, controlled, clinical trial to compare the efficacy of prophylactic rinses in reducing the salivary load of SARS-CoV-2 for up to two hours post rinsing. We compared the cycle threshold (Ct) values compared in saliva samples between the groups and within the groups at baseline (pre-rinse), zero hours, one hour and two hours post rinse, using SARS-CoV-2 reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) analysis. We aim to identify a safe and economical way of reducing the potential spread of COVID-19 from patient to providers and staff through pre-procedural rinses and furthermore, determine which rinse, if any, is the most effective in doing so. The study was opened to recruitment in October 2020. However, due to low subject recruitment rate from the hospitalised population, the protocol was amended to include remote study visits. For the later cohort, subject eligibility was assessed via telephone and subjects consented over a virtual platform using the guidelines provided by AU Institutional Review Board. Once consent was obtained, a study kit was delivered to the subject's location. Study samples were self-collected under the observation of a study team member and stored on ice until collection. Most subjects were recruited remotely between February and June 2021. Patients included in this clinical trial were at least 18 years old, could understand English, were either non-symptomatic or symptomatic but not intubated, and self-reported no allergies to Listerine, PI, or CHX. In addition, patients willing to do remote visits required access to video conference technology. A total of 32 COVID-19 patients consented to the trial. Informed consent was obtained from all subjects, all subjects were able to consent for themselves, and were able to withdraw from the study if desired at any time. The study design was reviewed and approved by the Institutional Review Board of AU (protocol number 1607808) and the Human Subjects Ethics Board of AU and was conducted in accordance with the Helsinki Declaration of 1975. fetched_contents.text: Oral Antiseptics against SARS-CoV-2: A Literature Review Abstract Dentists are health care workers with the highest risk of exposure to COVID-19, because the oral cavity is considered to be a reservoir for SARS-CoV-2 transmission. The identification of SARS-CoV-2 in saliva, the generation of aerosols, and the proximity to patients during dental procedures are conditions that have led to these health care workers implementing additional disinfection strategies for their protection. Oral antiseptics are widely used chemical substances due to their ability to reduce the number of microorganisms. Although there is still no evidence that they can prevent the transmission of SARS-CoV-2, some preoperative oral antiseptics have been recommended as control measures, by different health institutions worldwide, to reduce the number of microorganisms in aerosols and droplets during dental procedures. Therefore, this review presents the current recommendations for the use of oral antiseptics against SARS-CoV-2 and analyzes the different oral antiseptic options used in dentistry. Keywords: COVID-19, SARS-CoV-2, oral antiseptic, infection control 1. Introduction Coronavirus disease 19 (COVID-19), responsible for the pandemic that began in late 2019 in Wuhan, China, is caused by a virus that originated as a new type-2 severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), and there have been more than 536 million confirmed cases up to June 2022 [1,2]; the main transmission route is through direct contact or the inhalation of aerosols [3]. The Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) of the United States Department of Labor established an occupational risk pyramid for COVID-19, which is structured into four levels of risk exposure: very high, high, medium, and low. Health workers are considered a group with a very high risk of exposure, because their procedures can generate aerosols; this particularly includes dentists, due to the close contact with patients and the instruments used [4]. Dentists present the greatest risk of exposure to COVID-19 infection. The dental devices and instruments utilized, such as ultrasonic devices, implant and surgical motors, hand pieces, and triple syringes, can generate large amounts of aerosols, which can disperse numerous bacteria and viruses [5]. All of this has prompted dental care workers to pay more attention to their protective barriers against SARS-CoV-2, including larger particle filtration masks, caps, respirators, and face shields [6,7]. However, despite these additional measures, the presence of SARS-CoV-2 has been identified in different types of materials, remaining in plastic for up to 4 days, and 7 days in stainless-steel and surgical masks [8]. The high risk of virus transmission, together with the existence of asymptomatic patients, forces dentists to consider all patients as potentially infected [5]. In addition, some health institutions worldwide, such as the National Health Commission (NHC) of the People’s Republic of China, the National Administration of Traditional Chinese Medicine, the Center for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), The Association of Cantonal Dentists in Switzerland (VKZS) and the Swiss Dental Association (SSO) [9], the American Dental Association (ADA) [10], and the World Health Organization (WHO) [7], have recommended the use of oral antiseptics as agents that can reduce the viral load of SARS-CoV-2 before dental procedures [11]. Thus, the aim of the present study was to evaluate some of the antiseptic agents most frequently used by dental professionals and their antiviral effects against SARS-CoV-2 from both in vitro and in vivo studies to identify the most common compounds effective in reducing the viral load in the oral cavity in people infected with the virus. 2. Structure of SARS-CoV-2 Coronaviruses are a group of non-segmented positive-strand enveloped RNA viruses. SARS-CoV-2 particles have a spherical shape with diameters ranging from 60 to 140 nm and are coated with 9 to 12 nm spike proteins along with viral envelope proteins that give it the appearance of a crown [3]. The virus has a tropism for cells that have two specific receptors: angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) [12] and transmembrane serine protease-2 (TMPRSS2), which are mainly present in the lungs [13]. These receptors have been identified in epithelial cells of the tongue (spinous cell layer, stratum corneum, and epithelial surface), gingival tissues, oral mucosa, taste cells of human fungiform papillae, and salivary glands (ductal, acinar, and myoepithelial cells); thus, the oral cavity has gained relevance in the pathogenesis of the disease [13,14,15]. 3. Importance of the Transmission and Pathogenicity of SARS-CoV-2 in the Oral Cavity The highest SARS-CoV-2 viral loads are found in the nasal cavity, nasopharynx, and oropharynx in relation to the high expression of the ACE2 receptor [15]. The mouth is part of the oropharynx, and harbors bacteria and viruses from the nose, throat, respiratory tract, and contaminated saliva, which can spread viral infections [16]. In the first phase of COVID-19 infection (first 10 days), the patient is usually asymptomatic but highly contagious, and the virus accumulates mainly in the nasal, oral, and pharyngeal areas. The number of ACE2 receptors is greater in the salivary glands and in the mucosa of the tongue compared with the lungs and saliva droplets, which is why they represent the most relevant route of transmission [17]. The presence of the virus has been detected in 91.7% of saliva samples from patients with COVID-19, highlighting the importance of the oral cavity in the transmission and reservoir of SARS-CoV-2 [18]. Infection control in dental practice during the COVID-19 pandemic represents a challenge, because SARS-CoV-2 can be transmitted through aerosols produced by breathing, speaking, coughing, and sneezing [19]. fetched_contents.text: Chlorhexidine in Dentistry: Pharmacology, Uses, and Adverse Effects Abstract Objectives The aim of this work was to review the current uses of chlorhexidine (CHX) in dentistry based on its mechanism of action, whilst highlighting the most effective protocols that render the highest clinical efficacy whilst limiting adverse drug reactions. Methods A literature search was conducted using the key words chlorhexidine, mechanism of action, adverse effects, and dentistry using databases in the University of Toronto library system. The titles and abstracts were read, and relevant articles were selected. Results A total of 1100 publications were identified, 100 were investigated, and 67 of them were used. Out of the 67 selected articles, 12 were reviews on CHX; 5 articles focussed on CHX gels; 13 focussed on CHX mouthwashes; 8 focussed on CHX products; 13 discussed adverse effects associated with CHX; 13 focussed on periodontal pathology and treatment; 6 focussed on implant periodontal and dental surgeries; 7 evaluated effects on caries; 6 looked at the mechanisms of action; and 12 focussed on the antibacterial and antimicrobial impact on the oral biome. There were multiple areas of overlap amongst the articles, and results showed that CHX provides different uses, but mainly as an adjunct to various treatments. Mouthwash was the most superior medium when used in short time spans when mechanical prophylaxis was not possible for the prevention of gingivitis and maintenance of oral hygiene. CHX products are often used in periodontics, post–oral surgical procedures, and as a prophylaxis for multiple invasive procedures with minimal adverse effects. Tooth staining was the most negative adverse effect reported by patients. Conclusions CHX's antimicrobial properties make it an ideal prophylactic when mechanical debridement is not possible. CHX mouthwash appears to be more effective compared to gels. Concentrations of 0.12% to 0.2% are recommended; any mouthwash with concentrations above 0.2% will unnecessarily increase the unwanted side effects. CHX is useful amongst various areas of dentistry including oral surgery, periodontics, and even general dentistry. For long-term treatments, especially in periodontitis patients (stage I-III) undergoing nonsurgical treatments, CHX chips are recommended. CHX chips are also recommended as an adjunct to implant debridement in patients with peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis over CHX mouthwash and gels. Key words: Chlorhexidine, Mechanism of action, Adverse effects, Dentistry Introduction Chlorhexidine (CHX) is a bisbiguanide that was developed in the 1940s in the UK and has been marketed as a general disinfectant.1 In the 1970s, its antiplaque activity was discovered, and by 1976 it was available as a mouthwash.1,2 Oral biofilm and its associated bacteria have been linked to the pathogenesis of various oral diseases including halitosis, caries, gingivitis, and periodontitis.3, 4, 5 Periodontal disease in the US has been diagnosed in approximately 47.2% of adults 30 years and older and 70.1% of adults 65 years of age and older.6,7 Therefore, biofilm control is critical to prevent the development of such conditions; specifically, manual or electronically powered toothbrushing is recommended as the main method for prevention as well as reduction of plaque and gingivitis.3, 4, 5,7,8 Effective mechanical biofilm control requires time, willingness, and dexterity-related skills.3,4 However, this may not be feasible in patients who are mentally or physically disabled, as well as in postsurgical situations where oral hygiene becomes almost impossible.2, 3, 4,9,10 Currently, CHX mouthwash is the most potent chemotherapeutic agent and gold standard in reducing S mutans and oral biofilm.11,12 In dentistry, CHX products are available by prescription and include formulations such as mouthwashes, gels, chips, and varnishes. 1,13,14 There are many scholarly articles and manufacturer reports describing the uses and benefits of CHX products; however, there are conflicting data amongst them. Moreover, there is limited clinical information regarding effective protocols. This review will examine the mechanism of action (MOA) of CHX and investigate the most effective protocols regarding CHX uses in dentistry whilst highlighting important adverse drug reactions (ADRs) relevant to a dental setting based on the most recent literature and clinical trials. Amongst protocols, general, periodontal, prophylactic, and postsurgical uses of CHX will be investigated and addressed and any associated ADRs examined. Methods A literature review was commenced to identify the MOA and to investigate the most effective adjunctive uses of CHX in dental procedures. Such procedures include the treatment of periodontal diseases as well as prophylactic uses. Databases in the University of Toronto library system were searched to locate relevant peer-reviewed articles written in English and published in the past 5 years. Search words entered included “chlorhexidine,” “mechanism of action,” “adverse effects,” and “dentistry.” Dentistry textbooks were also obtained from the National Dental Examination Board as well as the University of Toronto Library and reviewed for relevant information. A total of 1100 publications were identified, the abstracts were read, and out of the 1100 a total of 100 were investigated. Analysis of articles revealed that CHX mouthwash is the most effective out of the CHX products due to its ability to successfully inhibit significantly more plaque when compared with gels and varnishes.14, 15, 16, 17 Therefore, this review will focus on CHX mouthwashes. Evidence supporting reduced transmission risk in dental settings is indirect rather than direct in most of the available studies. The search results indicate that the literature often infers transmission risk from reductions in viral load, aerosol generation, or contamination, rather than from randomized trials measuring actual transmission events [N2-F2][N3-F3]. For example, the British Dental Journal review explicitly states that pre-procedural mouth rinses are used to reduce viral loads as recommended by the ADA, but that “there was little empirical data to support pre-procedural rinses to reduce COVID-19 transmission to healthcare professionals or patients” at the time of the study [N2-F2]. The same source also notes that existing data provide evidence for efficacy in reducing bacterial and viral loads in in vitro cell cultures, oral cavities, and aerosols, but that the hypothesis remains supported indirectly rather than directly proven [N2-F2].

The interventions compared with controls in the dental literature are typically mouthwashes versus water or no rinse, and sometimes against controls that do not include an active antiseptic. In the 2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load, participants were randomized to one of five treatment groups: 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHX), 1.5% hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), 1% povidone-iodine (PI), Listerine, or water [N2-F2]. The study measured salivary viral load by cycle threshold (Ct) values and aimed to determine whether any rinse reduced salivary SARS-CoV-2 load over time, rather than directly measuring transmission risk [N2-F2]. The review also states that recent systematic reviews strongly support the hypothesis that prophylactic rinses can reduce oral viral load, but that evidence does not yet directly prove reduced in-office spread of viruses [N2-F2]. This means the relative risk reduction for transmission is not directly quantified in the cited evidence; instead, the literature treats viral load reduction as a proxy for reduced transmission potential [N2-F2][N3-R3].

Transmission risk in dental clinics is estimated by examining aerosol-generating procedures, droplet generation, and environmental contamination. The dental literature in the shared dependencies emphasizes that aerosol generation is a major concern in dental settings, with procedures such as ultrasonic devices, implant and surgical motors, hand pieces, and triple syringes producing large amounts of aerosols [N3-F3]. The review also notes that SARS-CoV-2 can be transmitted through aerosols, respiratory droplets, and contact with contaminated surfaces [N3-F3]. In the 2025 study mentioned in the search results, the aim was to evaluate the effect of aerosol dispersion on SARS-CoV-2 viral load during routine operations in a restorative dental clinic [N7-R1]. This suggests that transmission risk is estimated through aerosol dispersion during specific dental procedures rather than through direct patient-to-patient contact in a clinic setting [N7-R1]. Similarly, the evidence on saliva and aerosol transmission indicates that viral load is often measured in saliva, aerosols, or surface contamination, with the goal of understanding how these pathways contribute to risk [N2-F2][N7-R3].

Overall, the evidence base is mixed. Some sources support the indirect inference that mouth rinses can reduce viral load and thus plausibly lower transmission risk, while others caution that the evidence is not yet direct and that many studies are limited by indirect outcome measurement [N2-F2][N3-R3]. The reviewed evidence does not provide a single large relative risk reduction across all studies; instead, the literature suggests a range of interventions and a need for more direct transmission studies [N2-F2][N3-F3].

The clinical context and limitations in the evidence largely weaken the interpretation of antiseptic rinses as a definitive intervention. First, study design limitations include small sample sizes and short durations. The 2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load enrolled only 32 patients and excluded many due to insufficient baseline saliva volume, leaving a final sample size of 6–10 patients per group [N2-F2]. This is a classic limitation of clinical trials in infectious disease settings: small numbers make it difficult to detect meaningful differences and increase the risk of false positives or negatives. The same study also mentions that results were compared at baseline, zero hours, one hour, and two hours post-rinse, indicating a relatively short observation window [N2-F2]. Short duration may limit conclusions about sustained effects or whether any benefit lasts long enough to be clinically meaningful during a dental procedure [N2-F2].

Second, the evidence does not consistently apply to routine dental procedures versus emergency or high-risk cases. The reviewed sources describe recommendations for pre-procedural rinses in routine dental settings and during aerosol-generating procedures, but they also emphasize that the evidence for transmission reduction is still limited [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The literature review notes that dentists are at high risk due to close contact with patients and aerosol-generating equipment, and that some health institutions recommend antiseptics as control measures during dental procedures [N3-F3]. However, the evidence base is still described as weak and mostly indirect, which means the findings are more relevant to routine procedures than to emergency or extremely high-risk scenarios where aerosol generation is maximal [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The 2025 study on aerosol dispersion during routine operations in a restorative dental clinic supports the idea that procedure-specific settings matter [N7-R1], but it does not establish a broad rule across all dental contexts.

Third, patient adherence and protocol fidelity likely affect real-world effectiveness. The clinical trial in the shared evidence relied on patients rinsing with water before saliva collection and then being assigned to rinse with one of the mouthwashes [N2-F2]. This suggests that adherence depends on patient compliance with the study protocol, which may not be fully replicable outside a controlled trial. In the review, it is also stated that many clinical studies assess viral load reduction based on RT-qPCR results without accounting for viral infectivity, which implies that even if a mouthwash reduces detectable viral RNA, it may not reduce actual infectious virus [N1-F1]. This further limits the real-world applicability of findings: if patients do not rinse properly, do not rinse long enough, or rinse with diluted or incorrect formulations, the benefit may be lost [N2-F2]. The safety evidence also highlights that some adverse effects, such as tooth staining and oral irritation, may influence adherence, especially with long-term or frequent use [N5-F4].

Overall, the evidence is best interpreted as encouraging but cautious. It supports the use of antiseptic rinses in routine dental care as a potential control measure, but the limitations—small samples, short duration, indirect outcomes, and reliance on adherence—mean that real-world effectiveness remains uncertain and cannot be overinterpreted [N2-F2][N3-F3][N5-F4].

The evidence for viral load reduction after antiseptic rinses is strongest for in vitro studies and weaker for in vivo studies, with some in vivo results not supporting the expected benefit. In vitro evidence shows that several oral antiseptics have virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2, including chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, and some mouthwash components [N1-R4][N4-R4]. The 2020 in vitro study cited in the search results reports that povidone-iodine gargle and mouthwash, undiluted and at 1:2 dilution, demonstrated potent and rapid virucidal activity with ≥4 log10 reduction of viral titre in 15 minutes [N6-R2]. Another in vitro study notes that povidone-iodine was effective in killing SARS-CoV-2 and had higher virucidal activity than other commonly used active ingredients [N6-R3]. The literature review also states that chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine have been examined in systematic reviews and meta-analyses for their effects on viral load, suggesting broader support for these agents in the antiseptic category [N4-R1][N4-R4].

In vivo evidence is more mixed. The 2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load found that, in comparison with no rinse, sodium chloride (NaCl) was the most effective mouth rinse for reducing viral load [N1-R1]. However, the same source also notes that the study was a systematic review and that the evidence base is still limited [N1-R1]. The randomized clinical trial on antiseptic mouthwashes versus placebo found that salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes, even though in vitro evidence suggested virucidal activity [N1-F1]. This is a key limitation: the in vivo study did not show a measurable reduction in viral load, while the in vitro evidence did [N1-F1]. The trial’s results therefore indicate that some mouthwashes may work in the lab but not in practice, at least in this setting [N1-F1].

Regarding dose dependence, the evidence is uneven. The in vitro evidence for povidone-iodine suggests potent virucidal activity at undiluted and 1:2 dilution, indicating that potency may depend on concentration [N6-R2][N6-R3]. The literature review also notes that a 50% v/v dilution of chlorhexidine gluconate or alcohol and essential oils was necessary for complete inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infectivity, suggesting that concentration matters for effectiveness [N4-R4]. However, the in vivo study does not report dose-dependent effects in the way the question requires, so the evidence for dose dependence in practice is weaker than in vitro [N1-F1].

As for specificity, the evidence suggests that the effect is mostly specific to SARS-CoV-2 rather than broad antiviral activity, at least in the studies reviewed. The evidence base supports the idea that oral antiseptic rinses may reduce **SARS-CoV-2 viral load**, especially in **in vitro** studies, but the evidence for **reduced transmission risk during dental procedures** is more limited and mostly **indirect**. Overall, the most defensible conclusion is that antiseptic rinses can reduce viral load in some settings and may lower the risk of transmission, but the evidence is not strong enough to claim certainty or broad applicability in routine dental practice.

---

## 1) Viral load reduction after antiseptic rinses

The strongest evidence is **in vitro**, where several antiseptics have shown measurable reduction in SARS-CoV-2 viral load or infectivity. The branch report states that in vitro studies show virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2, including **chlorhexidine**, **povidone-iodine**, and some mouthwash components [N1-R4][N4-R4]. One in vitro study reported that **povidone-iodine gargle and mouthwash**, undiluted and at 1:2 dilution, demonstrated **≥4 log10 reduction of viral titre** in 15 minutes [N6-R2]. Another in vitro study found that povidone-iodine was effective in killing SARS-CoV-2 and had higher virucidal activity than other commonly used active ingredients [N6-R3]. A broader literature review also notes that chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine have been examined in systematic reviews and meta-analyses for their effects on viral load [N4-R1][N4-R4].

However, the in vivo evidence is **mixed and less supportive**. The branch report notes that the **2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load** found that, compared with no rinse, **sodium chloride (NaCl)** was the most effective mouth rinse for reducing viral load [N1-R1]. But the same source also says the evidence base is still limited [N1-R1]. The randomized clinical trial on antiseptic mouthwashes versus placebo found that **salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes**, despite in vitro evidence of virucidal activity [N1-F1]. This is an important caution: **in vitro benefit does not always translate to in vivo benefit**.

On **dose dependence**, the evidence is uneven. The in vitro evidence suggests potency at undiluted and 1:2 dilution for povidone-iodine [N6-R2][N6-R3], while the literature review notes that a **50% v/v dilution** of chlorhexidine gluconate or alcohol and essential oils was necessary for complete inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infectivity [N4-R4]. But the in vivo study does not provide clear dose-dependent findings, so the evidence for dose dependence in practice is weaker [N1-F1].

As for **specificity**, the evidence suggests the effect is mostly **specific to SARS-CoV-2** rather than broad antiviral activity. The literature review explicitly states that the goal was to evaluate antiseptics against SARS-CoV-2 and that results were compared with a placebo group using water [N1-F1]. It also notes that in vitro studies often assess virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2, while in vivo studies may assess viral load reduction without direct evidence of antiviral activity against other viruses [N1-F1]. The mechanism evidence further supports virus-specific action, with the underlying mechanism tied to the sensitivity of the viral envelope to chemical agents such as **ethanol, chlorhexidine, and povidone-iodine** [N4-R2].

## 2) Reduced aerosol or saliva-borne viral load during dental procedures

The evidence supports the idea that antiseptic rinses may lower contamination in **saliva and aerosols**, but the magnitude of reduction and measurement methods differ across studies. The branch report states that studies often measure **aerosol, saliva, or surface contamination** rather than transmission risk directly [N2-F2][N7-R1]. The 2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load measured salivary viral load by **cycle threshold (Ct) values** after pre-procedural rinses [N2-F2]. A separate study on aerosol dispersion during routine operations in a restorative dental clinic aimed to evaluate the effect of aerosol dispersion on SARS-CoV-2 viral load during dental procedures [N7-R1].

Magnitude of reduction varies widely. The strongest reported reduction is in vitro: **≥4 log10 reduction of viral titre** with undiluted and 1:2 dilution povidone-iodine gargle and mouthwash [N6-R2]. In contrast, the clinical trial reported that **sodium chloride was the most effective mouth rinse for reducing viral load** compared with no rinse, but it does not quantify the exact magnitude of reduction [N1-R1]. The infectivity study found that **cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC)** significantly reduced viral infectivity at **1-hour post-mouthwash**, but the overall salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes [N1-F1]. This pattern shows that some settings show substantial reduction, while others show limited or no benefit.

Quantification differs by study. In the clinical trial, viral load was measured by **RT-qPCR Ct values** at multiple timepoints [N2-F2]. In the in vitro study, viral titre was reduced by **≥4 log10**, a standard microbiological measure [N6-R2]. In the infectivity study, viral load was quantified by RT-qPCR and infectious viral load was evaluated by incubating saliva in cell cultures [N1-F1]. This means the literature uses both **quantitative PCR** and **infectivity assays**, but the latter is less common and harder to standardize [N1-F1].

## 3) Reduced transmission risk in dental settings

Evidence for reduced transmission risk is **indirect** rather than direct. Most studies infer risk reduction from viral load reduction, aerosol generation, or contamination rather than from direct transmission events [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The branch report notes that the literature often infers transmission risk from reductions in viral load, aerosol generation, or contamination, rather than from randomized trials measuring actual transmission events [N2-F2][N3-F3]. This suggests that transmission risk is estimated through **procedure-specific aerosol dispersion** and not through direct patient-to-patient contact in a clinic setting [N7-R1].

## 4) Clinical context and limitations

The clinical context and limitations substantially shape interpretation. First, **study design limitations** include **small sample size, short duration, and non-dental populations** in some studies. The 2023 clinical trial enrolled only **32 patients**, and many were excluded due to insufficient baseline saliva volume, leaving **6–10 patients per group** [N2-F2]. This is a classic limitation in infectious disease studies and makes it difficult to detect meaningful differences or generalize findings. The study also measured outcomes at baseline, zero hours, one hour, and two hours post-rinse, indicating a relatively short observation window [N2-F2]. Short duration may limit conclusions about sustained effects or whether any benefit lasts long enough to be clinically meaningful during a dental procedure [N2-F2].

Second, the evidence does not consistently apply to **routine dental procedures versus emergency or high-risk cases**. The reviewed sources describe recommendations for pre-procedural rinses in routine dental settings and during aerosol-generating procedures, but they also emphasize that the evidence for transmission reduction is still limited [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The literature review notes that dentists are at high risk due to close contact with patients and aerosol-generating equipment, and that some health institutions recommend antiseptics as control measures during dental procedures [N3-F3]. However, the evidence base is described as weak and mostly indirect, so the findings are more relevant to routine procedures than to emergency or extremely high-risk scenarios [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The aerosol dispersion study supports the idea that procedure-specific settings matter [N7-R1], but it does not establish a broad rule across all dental contexts.

Third, **patient adherence and protocol fidelity** likely affect real-world effectiveness. The clinical trial in the shared evidence relied on patients rinsing with water before saliva collection and then being assigned to rinse with one of the mouthwashes [N2-F2]. This suggests that adherence depends on patient compliance with the study protocol, which may not be fully replicable outside a controlled trial. The literature review also notes that many clinical studies assess viral load reduction based on RT-qPCR results without accounting for viral infectivity, implying that even if a mouthwash reduces detectable viral RNA, it may not reduce actual infectious virus [N1-F1]. This further limits real-world applicability: if patients do not rinse properly, do not rinse long enough, or rinse with diluted or incorrect formulations, the benefit may be lost [N2-F2].

Safety and side effects also matter. The branch report notes that **chlorhexidine mouthwash** can cause **tooth staining, dry mouth, taste alteration, numbness, pain, and other mucosal irritation** [N5-F4]. These side effects may influence adherence, especially with long-term or frequent use [N5-F4]. While the evidence does not show widespread harm in the reviewed studies, it does highlight that routine use is not without practical concerns [N5-F4].

## 5) Bottom line: what can be concluded?

- **Yes, the evidence supports viral load reduction** after antiseptic rinses, especially in **in vitro** studies for **chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, and some mouthwash components** [N1-R4][N4-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3].  
- **In vivo evidence is mixed and less supportive**, with some studies showing no detectable reduction in salivary viral load [N1-F1].  
- **Aerosol and saliva contamination are plausible targets** for intervention, but the magnitude of reduction varies, and measurement methods differ [N2-F2][N7-R1][N6-R2].  
- **Transmission risk is inferred indirectly**, not measured directly, and the evidence does not show a direct relative risk reduction for transmission [N2-F2][N3-F3].  
- **Clinical context and limitations are important**: small samples, short duration, adherence issues, and safety concerns weaken overinterpretation [N2-F2][N5-F4].

## 6) Practical conclusion

For dental practice, the best-supported interpretation is that **oral antiseptic rinses may help reduce SARS-CoV-2 viral load in some settings and may lower the risk of transmission indirectly by reducing aerosol and saliva contamination**, but the evidence is not strong enough to claim that they are a definitive or universally effective intervention. In routine dental procedures, they may be a useful control measure, especially when combined with other infection control practices such as personal protective equipment, physical distancing, and aerosol-reducing techniques [N2-F2][N3-F3]. However, clinicians should not overstate the evidence and should recognize that the benefits are likely **modest, context-dependent, and subject to real-world adherence and safety constraints** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

- **Transmission risk is inferred indirectly**, not measured directly, and the evidence does not show a direct relative risk reduction for transmission [N2-F2][N3-F3].  
- **Clinical context and limitations are important**: small samples, short duration, adherence issues, and safety concerns weaken overinterpretation [N2-F2][N5-F4].

For dental practice, the best-supported interpretation is that **oral antiseptic rinses may help reduce SARS-CoV-2 viral load in some settings and may lower the risk of transmission indirectly by reducing aerosol and saliva contamination**, but the evidence is not strong enough to claim that they are a definitive or universally effective intervention. The evidence base supports the idea that oral antiseptic rinses may reduce **SARS-CoV-2 viral load**, especially in **in vitro** studies, but the evidence for **reduced transmission risk during dental procedures** is more limited and mostly **indirect**. Overall, the most defensible conclusion is that antiseptic rinses can reduce viral load in some settings and may lower the risk of transmission, but the evidence is not strong enough to claim certainty or broad applicability in routine dental practice.

---

## 1) Viral load reduction after antiseptic rinses

The strongest evidence is **in vitro**, where several antiseptics have shown measurable reduction in SARS-CoV-2 viral load or infectivity. The branch report states that in vitro studies show virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2, including **chlorhexidine**, **povidone-iodine**, and some mouthwash components [N1-R4][N4-R4]. One in vitro study reported that **povidone-iodine gargle and mouthwash**, undiluted and at 1:2 dilution, demonstrated **≥4 log10 reduction of viral titre** in 15 minutes [N6-R2]. Another in vitro study found that povidone-iodine was effective in killing SARS-CoV-2 and had higher virucidal activity than other commonly used active ingredients [N6-R3]. A broader literature review also notes that chlorhexidine and povidone-iodine have been examined in systematic reviews and meta-analyses for their effects on viral load [N4-R1][N4-R4].

However, the in vivo evidence is **mixed and less supportive**. The branch report notes that the **2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load** found that, compared with no rinse, **sodium chloride (NaCl)** was the most effective mouth rinse for reducing viral load [N1-R1]. But the same source also says the evidence base is still limited [N1-R1]. The randomized clinical trial on antiseptic mouthwashes versus placebo found that **salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes**, despite in vitro evidence of virucidal activity [N1-F1]. This is an important caution: **in vitro benefit does not always translate to in vivo benefit**.

On **dose dependence**, the evidence is uneven. The in vitro evidence suggests potency at undiluted and 1:2 dilution for povidone-iodine [N6-R2][N6-R3], while the literature review notes that a **50% v/v dilution** of chlorhexidine gluconate or alcohol and essential oils was necessary for complete inhibition of SARS-CoV-2 infectivity [N4-R4]. But the in vivo study does not provide clear dose-dependent findings, so the evidence for dose dependence in practice is weaker [N1-F1].

As for **specificity**, the evidence suggests the effect is mostly **specific to SARS-CoV-2** rather than broad antiviral activity. The literature review explicitly states that the goal was to evaluate antiseptics against SARS-CoV-2 and that results were compared with a placebo group using water [N1-F1]. It also notes that in vitro studies often assess virucidal activity against SARS-CoV-2, while in vivo studies may assess viral load reduction without direct evidence of antiviral activity against other viruses [N1-F1]. The mechanism evidence further supports virus-specific action, with the underlying mechanism tied to the sensitivity of the viral envelope to chemical agents such as **ethanol, chlorhexidine, and povidone-iodine** [N4-R2].

## 2) Reduced aerosol or saliva-borne viral load during dental procedures

The evidence supports the idea that antiseptic rinses may lower contamination in **saliva and aerosols**, but the magnitude of reduction and measurement methods differ across studies. The branch report states that studies often measure **aerosol, saliva, or surface contamination** rather than transmission risk directly [N2-F2][N7-R1]. The 2023 clinical trial on SARS-CoV-2 salivary viral load measured salivary viral load by **cycle threshold (Ct) values** after pre-procedural rinses [N2-F2]. A separate study on aerosol dispersion during routine operations in a restorative dental clinic aimed to evaluate the effect of aerosol dispersion on SARS-CoV-2 viral load during dental procedures [N7-R1].

Magnitude of reduction varies widely. The strongest reported reduction is in vitro: **≥4 log10 reduction of viral titre** with undiluted and 1:2 dilution povidone-iodine gargle and mouthwash [N6-R2]. In contrast, the clinical trial reported that **sodium chloride was the most effective mouth rinse for reducing viral load** compared with no rinse, but it does not quantify the exact magnitude of reduction [N1-R1]. The infectivity study found that **cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC)** significantly reduced viral infectivity at **1-hour post-mouthwash**, but the overall salivary viral load was not affected by any of the four tested mouthwashes [N1-F1]. This pattern shows that some settings show substantial reduction, while others show limited or no benefit.

Quantification differs by study. In the clinical trial, viral load was measured by **RT-qPCR Ct values** at multiple timepoints [N2-F2]. In the in vitro study, viral titre was reduced by **≥4 log10**, a standard microbiological measure [N6-R2]. In the infectivity study, viral load was quantified by RT-qPCR and infectious viral load was evaluated by incubating saliva in cell cultures [N1-F1]. This means the literature uses both **quantitative PCR** and **infectivity assays**, but the latter is less common and harder to standardize [N1-F1].

## 3) Reduced transmission risk in dental settings

Evidence for reduced transmission risk is **indirect** rather than direct. Most studies infer risk reduction from viral load reduction, aerosol generation, or contamination rather than from direct transmission events [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The branch report notes that the literature often infers transmission risk from reductions in viral load, aerosol generation, or contamination, rather than from randomized trials measuring actual transmission events [N2-F2][N3-F3]. It also states that **there was little empirical data to support pre-procedural rinses to reduce COVID-19 transmission to healthcare professionals or patients** at the time of the study [N2-F2].

Interventions were usually compared with controls such as **mouthwashes versus water or no rinse**, and sometimes against controls that did not include an active antiseptic [N2-F2]. The 2023 clinical trial randomized patients to one of five treatment groups: 0.12% CHX, 1.5% H2O2, 1% PI, Listerine, or water [N2-F2]. The study aimed to determine whether any rinse reduced salivary SARS-CoV-2 load over time, rather than directly measuring transmission risk [N2-F2]. The review also says recent systematic reviews strongly support the hypothesis that prophylactic rinses can reduce oral viral load, but that evidence does not yet directly prove reduced in-office spread of viruses [N2-F2].

Transmission risk was estimated in dental clinics or simulated exposure settings by examining **aerosol-generating procedures, droplet generation, and environmental contamination** [N3-F3][N7-R3]. The literature emphasizes that **aerosol generation is a major concern** in dental settings, with procedures such as ultrasonic devices, implant and surgical motors, hand pieces, and triple syringes producing large amounts of aerosols [N3-F3]. The 2025 study on aerosol dispersion during routine operations in a restorative dental clinic tested aerosol generation in a clinical setting [N7-R1]. This suggests that transmission risk is estimated through **procedure-specific aerosol dispersion** and not through direct patient-to-patient contact in a clinic setting [N7-R1].

## 4) Clinical context and limitations

The clinical context and limitations substantially shape interpretation. First, **study design limitations** include **small sample size, short duration, and non-dental populations** in some studies. The 2023 clinical trial enrolled only **32 patients**, and many were excluded due to insufficient baseline saliva volume, leaving **6–10 patients per group** [N2-F2]. This is a classic limitation in infectious disease studies and makes it difficult to detect meaningful differences or generalize findings. The study also measured outcomes at baseline, zero hours, one hour, and two hours post-rinse, indicating a relatively short observation window [N2-F2]. Short duration may limit conclusions about sustained effects or whether any benefit lasts long enough to be clinically meaningful during a dental procedure [N2-F2].

Second, the evidence does not consistently apply to **routine dental procedures versus emergency or high-risk cases**. The reviewed sources describe recommendations for pre-procedural rinses in routine dental settings and during aerosol-generating procedures, but they also emphasize that the evidence for transmission reduction is still limited [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The literature review notes that dentists are at high risk due to close contact with patients and aerosol-generating equipment, and that some health institutions recommend antiseptics as control measures during dental procedures [N3-F3]. However, the evidence base is described as weak and mostly indirect, so the findings are more relevant to routine procedures than to emergency or extremely high-risk scenarios [N2-F2][N3-F3]. The aerosol dispersion study supports the idea that procedure-specific settings matter [N7-R1], but it does not establish a broad rule across all dental contexts.

Third, **patient adherence and protocol fidelity** likely affect real-world effectiveness. The clinical trial in the shared evidence relied on patients rinsing with water before saliva collection and then being assigned to rinse with one of the mouthwashes [N2-F2]. This suggests that adherence depends on patient compliance with the study protocol, which may not be fully replicable outside a controlled trial. The literature review also notes that many clinical studies assess viral load reduction based on RT-qPCR results without accounting for viral infectivity, implying that even if a mouthwash reduces detectable viral RNA, it may not reduce actual infectious virus [N1-F1]. This further limits real-world applicability: if patients do not rinse properly, do not rinse long enough, or rinse with diluted or incorrect formulations, the benefit may be lost [N2-F2].

Safety and side effects also matter. The branch report notes that **chlorhexidine mouthwash** can cause **tooth staining, dry mouth, taste alteration, numbness, pain, and other mucosal irritation** [N5-F4]. These side effects may influence adherence, especially with long-term or frequent use [N5-F4]. While the evidence does not show widespread harm in the reviewed studies, it does highlight that routine use is not without practical concerns [N5-F4].

## 5) Bottom line: what can be concluded?

- **Yes, the evidence supports viral load reduction** after antiseptic rinses, especially in **in vitro** studies for **chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, and some mouthwash components** [N1-R4][N4-R4][N6-R2][N6-R3].  
- **In vivo evidence is mixed and less supportive**, with some studies showing no detectable reduction in salivary viral load [N1-F1].  
- **Aerosol and saliva contamination are plausible targets** for intervention, but the magnitude of reduction varies, and measurement methods differ [N2-F2][N7-R1][N6-R2].  
- **Transmission risk is inferred indirectly**, not measured directly, and the evidence does not show a direct relative risk reduction for transmission [N2-F2][N3-F3].  
- **Clinical context and limitations are important**: small samples, short duration, adherence issues, and safety concerns weaken overinterpretation [N2-F2][N5-F4].

## 6) Practical conclusion

For dental practice, the best-supported interpretation is that **oral antiseptic rinses may help reduce SARS-CoV-2 viral load in some settings and may lower the risk of transmission indirectly by reducing aerosol and saliva contamination**, but the evidence is not strong enough to claim that they are a definitive or universally effective intervention. In routine dental procedures, they may be a useful control measure, especially when combined with other infection control practices such as personal protective equipment, physical distancing, and aerosol-reducing techniques [N2-F2][N3-F3]. However, clinicians should not overstate the evidence and should recognize that the benefits are likely **modest, context-dependent, and subject to real-world adherence and safety constraints** [N1-F1][N2-F2][N5-F4].
